Inventory levels are growing at a robust rate, according to the October Logistics Manager’s Index, which is at 70.7, up (+0.5) from September’s reading of 70.2.
This is the second-highest reading in four years, behind only June’s reading of 71.1.
Colorado State University, Florida Atlantic University, Rutgers University, and the University of Nevada, Reno, in conjunction with the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals (CSCMP), released the report on November 3.
The report offers the following analysis as excerpted below.
The index has now come in over 70.0 for three of the last five months; it had not cleared this threshold for over four years before this recent run.
This has been a year of expansion in the overall index, with average LMI readings coming in at 67.4. This is up significantly from 2025’s average of 58.7 and is the second-highest calendar-year average, behind only 2021, in the 10-year history of the index.
We also see significant expansion in Aggregate Logistics Costs in October, with the three cost/price metrics combining for a score of 257.5 (on a scale of 0-300), which is up (+11.4) from September’s reading of 246.1 this month.
This is the highest reading for this aggregate metric since March of 2022, when supply-driven inflation was rampant in the wake of both the cessation of COVID-era demand and the invasion of Ukraine. Given the pressure on logistics costs, it is likely that we will continue to see supply-driven inflation continue to increase in the near term.
No matter what happens with inflation in the future, it is clear that the inflation that has already occurred is impacting some consumers. The University of Michigan’s measure of U.S. consumer sentiment was down slightly (-0.1) to 48% in October.
This decline was driven almost entirely by buying conditions for durable goods, which were down 18% due to high interest rates and concerns regarding affordability. Consumer sentiment is down 15% since the start of the war with Iran and down 10% year-over-year – the “current economic conditions” metric is down 20% from October 2025.
Inventory Levels picked up in October, coming in notably higher (+8.0) at 66.9, which is their fastest rate of expansion since September of 2022. This was driven by movements in the second half of the month, when Inventory Levels expanded notably faster at 72.1 than the still fast – but more muted- rate of 61.8 in the first half of October.

Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work—I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today’s coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions.
The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That’s a lot of information to absorb.
It’s not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop!
It’s very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as “I’m not reading all of that”. It doesn’t matter how accurate or useful the information is, I’m instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me!
I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention.
I think I’ve found a low-effort way to do this that feels right.

I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted.
I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted :
I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse
Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file
This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster!
Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted:
Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation

What happens when students can one-shot last year’s homework? Inside CS146S and the engineering team at Monaco.
The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers . Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us are asking at work: what should a software engineer actually learn now?
Mihail Eric has two places to test his answer. He teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, where his colleagues use coding agents to ship software and investigate outages. I asked him to take us through the syllabus, then tell us which parts survived contact with his own engineering team.
This is also meant as a preview for all of you joining us in San Francisco for AIE Code next week, as required knowledge for all the conversations with the speakers, sponsors and attendees you’re about to have. If you can see this as a LS subscriber and haven’t got a ticket yet, you can use this code for 30% off (no refunds, sorry)
The first run of CS146S had nine assignments and a capstone. In one exercise, students ran an AI code reviewer on a repo and evaluated its feedback. By the next run, Mihail figured students could one-shot a lot of those exercises. When he asked a room of Stanford sophomores and juniors how they coded, everyone he surveyed was already using an agent.
So this time, part of the homework is contributing to an open-source project. The person who maintains the repo reviews the student’s patch. I like what that does to the assignment. You can ask an agent to implement a feature in an afternoon. You still have to find out whether the maintainer wants it, why the code behaves the way it does, and what else your patch might break. That conversation is also how a junior engineer gets to learn from a senior one.

datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages . I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table.
This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this:
This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means for everyone else their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away.
I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior...
And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely!

Comment My comment on Terry Pratchett's Study — Hacker News
Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich: https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin...
But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it.
